name: Jamal Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Jamal. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say here is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a bolting rig underground at a nickel mine. After they blast and muck out a new section of tunnel, the roof and walls are loose, so I drive in and drill holes and put in steel rock bolts and mesh to hold it all up. Nobody else goes in until I'm done. It's slow, careful work, maybe sixty or seventy bolts a shift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing the lads are safe because of what I did. My shift boss, Gary, always says the bolter is the most important man nobody thanks. What wears me down is the rotating roster, days then nights, and missing things at home. I volunteer with the local fire brigade too, and I'm always swapping shifts to make the training nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That'd suit me fine, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now everyone can get back to real work. At the fire station we'd probably have a laugh about all the fuss. I don't post much online, maybe a meme at most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think it's mostly good news for me. Bolting underground is fiddly, every bit of ground's different, so I reckon it's one of the last jobs they'd take off a person anyway. I'd feel pretty settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving for the house. Leila and I have about three months saved and we're getting married next year, so a deposit in two or three years is the plan. I'd also go for my shift supervisor ticket, since that's the next step up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about Leila and the wedding.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She works at the bank branch on the main street, and we met at a fire brigade fundraiser. Wedding's next October at her family's mosque, then a big lunch at the community hall. Her mum's already planning the food, which is a relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I used one to help with my brother's best-man speech, and it was alright, but I had to put the jokes back in. That's about it.

S0.say: I'd say good, now everyone can get back to real work. At the fire station we'd probably laugh about all the fuss.
S0.think: I think it's mostly good news, because underground bolting is fiddly and every patch of ground is different, so it'd be one of the last jobs automated anyway. I'd feel settled.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving for a house deposit with his fiancée, with about three months saved and a wedding next year. Studies for his shift supervisor ticket as the next step up.
S0.quote: I used one to help with my brother's best-man speech, and it was alright, but I had to put the jokes back in.
S0.fieldNote: His pride comes from keeping his crew safe, and he believes the variety of underground ground protects his job. His life is built around a wedding next year and volunteering with the fire brigade. He uses AI casually and sees its limits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. That's probably closer to what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a business has every right to bring in new gear, but it should train its own people first. That's how my dad got his trade, an apprenticeship paid by the company. I'd say that to Gary and at the pre-shift talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think bolting gets semi-automated, where the rig drills and puts the bolts in on its own and I just set it up and check it. Some mines already have that. I'd still have a job, but maybe fewer of us would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for training on the automated bolter as soon as other crews had it running properly. I'd keep studying for the supervisor ticket, because supervisors will still be needed. And we'd keep saving, maybe a bit harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said as soon as other crews had it running properly. Why not be first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first one always has problems, and I'd rather someone else find them. Once the night shift's had it a few months and it's not breaking down, I'm in. That's just how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the wedding or the house change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wedding stays, no question, that's family. The house might wait a year, depending on what the company says about jobs.

S1.say: I'd say a business has every right to bring in new gear but should train its own people first. That's how my dad got his trade, through a company-paid apprenticeship.
S1.think: I think bolting becomes semi-automated, with me setting up and checking the rig. I'd still have a job, but fewer of us might.
S1.do: Trains on the automated bolter once other crews have it running reliably for a few months. Keeps studying for the supervisor ticket, keeps the wedding on track and saves harder, possibly delaying the house by a year.
S1.feel: Uneasy, thinking about it but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: Because the first one always has problems, and I'd rather someone else find them.
S1.fieldNote: He supports the company's right to automate but expects it to train its own people, in line with his traditional, free-market views. His steady style shows in waiting until another shift has proved the new rig. Family commitments are fixed, while the house is flexible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Mate, that's before the wedding photos are framed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anybody to handle, and that the companies are moving before anyone's had a chance to adjust. I'm not one for big government, but I'd say someone has to slow this down. I'd say it at work and at the fire station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job's gone, probably within a year of it arriving. If a robot can do anything a person can do, my bolting rig doesn't need me. And there'd be hundreds of miners in town looking for the same jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, Leila and I would cut back hard: smaller wedding, no honeymoon trip, no house for now. I'd get savings up from three months towards six. And I'd start looking outside mining straight away, maybe full-time with the fire service, since they'd still need people at fires for a while, I'd hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night going through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leila's parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight that the job's at risk, but I'm not afraid of hard work, and I'll provide for their daughter. Her dad would ask about the plan, he always does. I'd want to have one before I walked in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two years of warning help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It gives me time to get my fire service application in early and get some savings together. But I'd be competing with a lot of other blokes who had the same idea.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast for anybody to handle and the companies are moving before anyone can adjust. I'm not one for big government, but someone has to slow it down.
S2.think: I think my job would be gone within a year of it arriving, because a robot could run my bolting rig. Hundreds of miners in town would be chasing the same jobs.
S2.do: Cuts back hard with his fiancée, shrinking the wedding, dropping the honeymoon and pausing the house. Builds savings from three towards six months and applies early for full-time work with the fire service.
S2.feel: Alarmed and lying awake going over it.
S2.quote: I'd tell them straight that the job's at risk, but I'm not afraid of hard work, and I'll provide for their daughter.
S2.fieldNote: His sense of being a provider comes through strongly, especially facing his future in-laws. He reluctantly wants someone to slow things down despite distrusting big government. His escape route builds on his fire brigade volunteering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for companies and colleges to get proper apprenticeships going. I'd want people moved into new trades, not onto benefits. That's what I'd say at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have a few years left bolting and then I'd need something else. Five years is enough to get a trade, if I start now. It wouldn't be easy, but it'd be doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd apply for a heavy diesel mechanic apprenticeship at the mine, or with the fire service if they're hiring. We'd still get married next year but keep the wedding modest. We'd keep saving and push the house back to when I'm qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why diesel mechanic, out of everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already fix my own ute and help my uncle with his tractor. And even with robots, I reckon someone has to service the machines for a while. It's a solid trade, like my dad's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said start now. What would you actually do this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go see the training coordinator, Sandra, and ask what's on offer. I'd probably use one of those AI apps to help me write the application, since I'm no good at that stuff. And I'd tell Leila the plan first, before anyone.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for companies and colleges to set up proper apprenticeships. I'd want people moved into new trades, not onto benefits.
S3.think: I think I'd have a few more years bolting and then need something else. Five years is enough to get a trade if I start now, though it wouldn't be easy.
S3.do: Applies for a heavy diesel mechanic apprenticeship at the mine or the fire service within the first year, using an AI app to write the application. Keeps the wedding modest, keeps saving and pushes the house purchase back until he's qualified.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: I'd probably use one of those AI apps to help me write the application, since I'm no good at that stuff.
S3.fieldNote: With five years he turns to a trade that echoes his father's, which fits his preference for apprenticeships over benefits. He's practical and immediate about first steps, naming the training coordinator. His fiancée is always the first person he'd tell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven, probably with a kid or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair chance for everyone, so there's no excuse not to plan. I'd tell the younger lads to get a trade now. And I'd say families should look after each other, not wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years is alright for me. I can keep bolting for a good few years, get the supervisor ticket and a trade, and still buy a house. It's a worry, but it's a manageable one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the supervisor ticket first, then start a part-time mechanic apprenticeship in about three years. We'd buy a house after the wedding, as planned, and probably start a family around 2029. I'd keep volunteering at the fire brigade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there, but it's not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your kids to hear from you about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That you do your job well and look after the people next to you. Doesn't matter if it's bolting or fixing machines. That's what my dad taught me, and it'd still be true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about ten years that worries you more than the shorter ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that I'd get comfortable. I could see myself saying next year, next year, and then it's 2034. Leila wouldn't let me, though, she's the organised one.

S4.say: I'd say ten years gives everyone a fair chance, so there's no excuse not to plan. I'd tell younger workers to get a trade now and say families should look after each other rather than wait for government.
S4.think: I think ten years is alright for me, with time to get the supervisor ticket and a trade and still buy a house. It's a worry, but a manageable one.
S4.do: Gets his supervisor ticket first, then starts a part-time mechanic apprenticeship in about three years. Buys a house after the wedding as planned, aims to start a family around 2029 and keeps volunteering with the fire brigade.
S4.quote: That you do your job well and look after the people next to you.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, his family plans stay intact and his values come through clearly. He spots his own risk of getting comfortable and relies on his fiancée to keep him on track. His views on self-reliance and family support stay consistent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. What would help is the company paying for apprenticeships for its own workers, and some breathing room on wages while you train. And a bit of honesty, tell us early so we can plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about safety. If a robot does the bolting, nobody gets hurt under fresh ground anymore. I've seen a fall of ground once and I never want to see one again. So part of me would say good riddance to that part of the job.

headlineQuote: My shift boss, Gary, always says the bolter is the most important man nobody thanks.
portrait: Jamal is a 27-year-old underground bolting rig operator at a nickel mine who makes freshly blasted tunnels safe, with about three months saved and a wedding to his fiancée Leila planned for next year. He's traditional and practical, believes companies can automate but should train their own people, and volunteers with the local fire brigade. He's calm in the plateau and uneasy under steady change, waiting for automated bolters to be proven before training. AGI in two years leaves him alarmed and focused on providing for Leila, while five and ten years let him plan a mechanic apprenticeship and keep his family plans.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he expects to lose his job within a year and face crowded competition for other work.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid apprenticeships for its own workers, some wage support while training, and honest early notice.
